The city council was asked to vote on what customarily would be a routine approval of an extension on an existing 10-year lease. Since its approval of the lease in November in a first reading, the council was asked to make decisions on a number of significant changes to the terms of the lease. On Monday night, the council decided not to move forward with the heavily modified lease proposal for the non-profit Piedmont Center for the Arts, which created the city’s first cultural arts center 10 years ago and has operated it since then at no cost to the city. Among the changes the council wanted was an increase in rent from $1 a year to $800 a month, a 30-day termination clause, and requirements to include non-arts related rentals as deemed appropriate by the city. These modifications were added following an approved first reading and a lengthy discussion with the prior council led by former mayor Bob McBain. The question Monday night instead became whether or not the city should become the “gatekeeper” of programs at 801 Magnolia Avenue, and if so, should there be a lease agreement at all? “A local, nonprofit group is not the best entity to be managing a city facility,” claimed Vice Mayor Tim Rood. “The way we approach our other [city-owned] rentals would apply here,” council member Jen Cavenaugh said. “Not once did anyone in PCA tell me that their goal was to manage a facility. articles.text: Guilty. Yesterday afternoon, April 20, ex-Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin was convicted of the second-degree unintentional murder, third-degree murder and second-degree manslaughter of George Floyd. In Piedmont a message of remembrance and support for Floyd was displayed at the Exedra: “Hold George Floyd in your heart today.” The five signs were spread out over the entire exedra facade, just as events on May 25, 2020 swept across the entire nation. “The conclusion of one of the most consequential trials in our country’s recent history undoubtedly leaves us all with many emotions and an understanding that while one step towards justice has been made, much work remains,” said Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. “The Piedmont Police Department is committed to continuing in this work together, with our community, through openness, professionalism, dignity and respect.” The trial began March 8, and testimony was heard from 45 witnesses, including bystanders, police officials and medical experts. In closing statements on April 19, Prosecutor Jerry Blackwell said, “There is a 46th witness... that witness is common sense.” A jury of seven women and five men deliberated for 10 hours before pronouncing Chauvin guilt on all accounts. Mr. Chauvin had been free on bail since October, but was put in handcuffs yesterday and ordered into custody by judge Peter Cahill. Minnesota’s sentencing guidelines recommend 12.5 years in prison for each murder charge and four years for the manslaughter. The state has asked for a tougher sentence than the recommendations provide. Chauvin’s sentencing will be in eight weeks.

articles.text: The city is close to meeting, and surpassing, the amount of housing units mandated by the RHNA (Regional Housing Needs Allocation) 2015-2023 cycle, according to a 2020 annual progress report. Piedmont has issued building permits for the construction of 73 new units out of a mandated 60 units by the end of next year, 2022. With changes in state legislation, however, it will “be challenging for the city to show that sufficient low and very low-income housing” is being produced, according to the report. That’s because most of the units that have received planning entitlements since the beginning of 2017 are allowed to be rented at market rates. To date, 12 very low income, 17 low income, 17 moderate, and 27 above moderate income level accessory dwelling units, or ADUs, have or are being constructed, for a total of 73 units. The current RHNA cycle mandates that 24 very low units be constructed - so Piedmont will still need to produce 12 “very low income” living units by the end of the cycle in 2022. “City staff has prepared a survey of local rents based on similar floor areas and amenities to substantiate the expected rents for moderate, low, and very low ADUs,” Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell told council members at Monday night’s City Council meeting, April 19. The survey found that average rents in Piedmont in 2020 total $2,590 a month, less than that reported for Oakland - which averaged at $2,705 for an approximately 780-square foot unit, or $3.47 per square foot. According to the state Department of Housing and Community Development, the allowable rents for very low-income units is between $1,143 for a studio, $1,305 for a one-bedroom, and $1,469 for a two-bedroom. In addition, Piedmont expects an RHNA 6th cycle of approximately 587 housing units, compared to 60 units in the current RHNA 5th cycle, representing a 979 percent increase. The expected allocation includes: 163 very low-income units, 94 low income units, 92 moderate income units, and 238 above moderate income units. The newly-minted Housing Advisory Committee held their first meeting last night, April 20. The purpose of the committee is to consider housing and equity issues in Piedmont, including the upcoming draft RHNA and the next housing element. To ensure that the city meets its housing needs assessment, it will seek a consulting firm; contractor Barry Miller, FAICP, prepared the city’s 3rd, 4th, and 5th RHNA, but has advised the city that he does not have the capacity to be the prime contractor on the city’s 6th cycle, given the significant increase in the RHNA, and need for a multi-disciplinary team to complete the work. Submission of the next cycle’s adopted Housing Element is due to The California Department of Housing and Community Development by January 2023. To meet this requirement, the city is listing Summer 2021 as a tentative due date for any RHNA appeals, and the first review of the draft housing element to take place in Summer 2022.

articles.text: Editor: How does a parent answer a child who asks, “does my life matter?” Or asks, “is Daddy racist?” With the Black Lives Matter and “woke” culture being ever-present in our everyday lives, this has created concerning issues in my household. As a Chinese mother raising children who are half White, I am asked on a continual basis those questions. My children are torn that being White in America means they are assumed to be racist while being Chinese means that they will face some form of discrimination or hate. There is no “middle” for my children. After recent conversations with fellow Piedmonters there was agreement that racial discrimination will always be present in society. I cannot count the number of times that I have either been shunned, ridiculed, physically or verbally attacked because of my race. My two most memorable experiences were being “jumped” by two Black kids on the outskirts of Oakland Chinatown when I was in elementary school; and being asked by a Piedmont police officer in the late 1980’s “do you speak English?” I hold no anger towards these individuals because those were my life experiences and I have persevered. Although I applaud Piedmont Unified School District for exposing students to the racial and economic inequalities that Black Americans experience, these teachings have created a profusion of “white guilt” for my children while they struggle to discern their Chinese side (especially during this period of increased Asian hate attacks). past and present-day race issues under the rug, but there should be limitations of these teachings by PUSD. articles.text: COVID-19 positivity increases slightly but week-over-week new cases drops Two new cases of COVID- 19 were reported in Piedmont in the past seven days, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data. While still low, positivity rates in the county crept upward as of Monday, April 19. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County rose slightly to 1.5 percent. On March 22, it was 1.1 percent, its lowest point since the coronavirus pandemic began over a year ago. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 85,468 – an increase of 676 new cases weekover-week, a slight decrease compared to recent weeks. In total, there have been 178 cases of COVID-19 recorded in Piedmont. There have been 26,589 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,329 cases in Hayward. Tragically, another 30 people have died of COVID-19 in Alameda County, bringing the total number of fatalities countywide to 1,477. The county is now several weeks into cautiously reopening after a dreadful winter surge of the disease. On March 30, Alameda County was moved into the orange tier, or moderate tier, the second-least restrictive tier in California’s color-coded four-tier protocol for reopening the state’s economy. To remain in the orange tier, the positivity rate needs to stay below 4.9 percent. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to stay below 3.9 – right now there are 3.3 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 5.2 percent – it is currently 1.9 percent in Alameda County. To move up into the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier, the cases per day need to be below 1 per 100,000 and the positivity rate needs to be below 2 percent. The positivity rate in low-income census tracts needs to be below 2.2 percent. Officials have said that Alameda County must meet orange tier benchmarks for at least three weeks before moving up tiers. The state could have moved the county up to the yellow tier yesterday, Tuesday, April 20, but no announcement has been made. All Bay Area counties other than Solano County are in the orange tier. Solano remains in the red tier. With the orange tier status, the capacity for indoor dining, retail, gyms, and offices increased and outdoor bars reopened. Indoor gatherings are discouraged by the state but are allowed in the orange tier. Only three households can gather at a time with face masks and social distancing. Museums, zoos and family entertainment centers all now have greater indoor capacity. Outdoor live events were permitted beginning this month. Indoor concerts, performances and other events were allowed Thursday, April 15 with restrictions. The entire color tier system is planned to be shuttered within a few months, though. Gov. articles.text: With COVID-19 vaccine eligibility open to all adults, Piedmont is closing in on total vaccination and leads Alameda County with more than 86 percent of its residents having received at least one dose of vaccine. Even though the use of a vaccine manufactured by Johnson & Johnson has been on pause since last week over blood clot concerns, vaccination in Alameda County has continued at a brisk pace. The Johnson & Johnson vaccine, which requires only one shot compared to the two-dose vaccines from Moderna and Pfizer, should return to circulation by this Friday, April 23, according to comments over the weekend from Dr. Anthony Fauci, the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommended that health agencies pause the use of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine last Tuesday, April 13 “out of an abundance of caution” due to reports of blood clotting issues in a handful of cases. The Alameda County Public Health Department announced the same day that it would stop administering Johnson & Johnson vaccines until further investigation. Almost 7 million doses of Johnson & Johnson vaccine have been administered in the United States. Six cases of the rare blood clot reaction have been recorded nationwide, and one death has been reported. The six cases of blood clots all occurred in women between the ages of 18 and 48. Symptoms occurred 6 to 13 days after vaccination. articles.text: Photo by Dick Carter Members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday group stopped on Sea View Avenue on April 14 for a group photo of some colorful tulips. Pictured are Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Sherry Jacobs, Nancy Henn, Brenda Ferrero, Bob and Kathy Gustafson, Harriette Louie, and Adrienne Hamlin. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group is back roaming the streets of Piedmont. On April 14th members of the group assembled at the Exedra for the first time in over a year. The pandemic made the group stop their walks over a year ago, but when Alameda County went to the Red/Tier 2 level on March 9th, the Recreation Department began the process of restarting the activity. A new set of safety protocols were developed that require registration, as well as social distancing, the use of masks, limited physical contact, and small size pods during the walks. The walk on April 14th marked the third anniversary of the group’s first walk in 2018. A total of 17 walkers had registered, but due to some schedule conflicts, 11 walkers were at the Exedra on Wednesday morning at 10 a.m. ready to reconnect with old friends and make some new ones. Participating were Nancy Henn, Bob Gustafson, Harriette Louie, Brenda Ferrero, Adrienne Hamlin, Nancy DeRoche, Dick Carter, and first time walkers Kathy Gustafson and Andree and Mark Greenberg. Dick Carter welcomed everyone. During its first two years almost 150 people had participated in the walks. He acknowledged that the weekly walks have provided not only physical activity but also a community for older adults where lasting friendships have been formed. April 14th was a beautiful spring morning with spring flowers in bloom, especially the fragrant cherry blossoms in full bloom in Piedmont Park. Dividing themselves into two groups (pods) they agreed on a route the walkers would take them to Sea View Avenue, one of their favorite destinations. But first, a Walk in the Park Before beginning Wednesday’s walk, the group walked through Piedmont Park, seeing the flowering cherry trees, the Japanese Tea House and the historical plaques. The group agreed this spot is a Piedmont treasure. The walkers went on Sierra Avenue to Sheridan and then to Wildwood, stopping to admire the profusion of flowers at the Davis house at the corner of Wildwood and Sheridan. Crossing the street, they went through the Hall Fenway, past Crocker Park and up to Sea View Avenue. They stopped for some photos of a front yard filled with colorful tulips before heading down Mountain Avenue. On Mountain they noticed a larger-than-life statue of a distinguished gentleman in the front yard of a home, something no one had noticed on previous walks on the street. To return to the Exedra, they took the somewhat hidden path connecting Mountain with Piedmont Court – and more cherry trees. Nancy DeRoche pointed out a home where she first lived in Piedmont. The house now has a birdhouse that matches the actual house and a metal sculpture of a bagpiper in its front yard. It was the first time on Piedmont Court for many of the walkers. The group finished their 2-1/2 mile walk in 90 minutes, a typical outing for the weekly walks. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues). Next Wednesday, April 28, they will meet at 10:15 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge, and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required. To sign up, click on https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu, or contact John Wilk at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov, for more information. Ngai was first appointed to the Commission in 2018. Her term as chair begins on April 26, 2021. She works in the office of the General Counsel of the Regents of the University of California at the UC Office of the President in Oakland. An expert in privacy, public disclosure laws, and education affairs, she advises senior Stella Ngai management, staff, and faculty at the 10 UC campuses. Previously, she was an Assistant District Attorney for the City and County of San Francisco, and also practiced law at the highly regarded San Francisco firm of Minami Tamaki.

articles.text: Beginning next Tuesday, April 27, high schools and middle school students will have the same class schedule. It consists of eight hours and 45 minutes of class time per week. High schoolers are on this schedule this week, while middle schoolers are on a “step-in” schedule this week of four to five hours of class. Piedmont elementary school students were the first in the city to return to in-class instruction in February. Since then, they have been on a schedule with nine hours of classroom instruction per week (two hours and 15 minutes, Tuesday through Friday). Though it represents less than one-third of a normal 28-30 hour-school week, getting to this schedule has been exhausting for everyone involved. Here is a chronological recap of Piedmont schools reopening. March 13, 2020: Piedmont School District close all schools as the first cases of COVID-19 are detected in the Bay Area. The initial shutdown plan is only for two weeks, March 16-27, and Piedmont is first school in Alameda County to announce closure. March 16: Class assignments move online to Schoology for grades 6-12; elementary students receive assignments on Google Docs. There is no minimum online “classtime” requirement or required attendance. Chromebooks are given out to all students in grades 6-12. March 25: Alameda County Office of Education requires all schools to stay closed through May 1. The State Department of Education drops the requirement of 180- day instructional day minimum. Piedmont has no plans of extending school year for lost days of instruction. March 31: California State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond announces schools in California will not reopen until fall 2020. May 14: Tony Thurmond announces that the decision of when and how to reopen public schools will be left to each school district. May 29: PHS holds in-person, masked and distanced graduation ceremonies in groups of 50-60 students at Witter Field; each student is allowed two guests from their household. No students give speeches. June 4: Piedmont’s School Reopening Task Force holds its first meeting with nearly 100 participants including 11 students, 20 parents, 12 classified community members, 46 certificated educators, 13 administrators, and two board members. June 26: “Piedmont Partners” starts a petition to reopen schools in the fall. 740 parents, students and community members sign the petition in four days. June 30: The School Board votes for a hybrid learning model for 2020-21 school year. The board approves in-person classes four or five days per week. July 13: The School Board directs the superintendent to start the school year online, Sixth graders Maya Sears (left) and Ruby Yasar create “automata” in a Makers Class by building a camshaft to twist and make their figures move. citing increases in Bay Area COVID cases. July 17: Governor Newsom decrees public schools cannot open if their county is on the COVID “Watch-List,” (now equivalent to the purple tier). Alameda County was put on the list July 12. August 17: The first day of school begins with online classes, with mandatory attendance and scheduled screen time. August 26: The district reaches a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with its teacher’s union solely for Distance Learning. Teachers receive a guarantee that in-person learning for TK-5th grade will not start before October 1. September 9: Piedmont teachers and the school district strike a tentative agreement for in-person learning based on a hybrid model. Cohort student sizes are limited to 15. The agreement would be activated if the County is in the red tier, and is not in a waiver of the K-5 plan. September 22: Alameda County moves to the red tier. Schools will have the green light to open after two weeks in the red tier. September 23: With a 3-2 vote, the School Board agrees to file a waiver with the county to allow TK-5th grade students back in school, regardless of COVID tier. The waiver program is later nullified by Alameda County. October 6: Piedmont’s School Board approves a school reopening plan. TK-2 students plan to return November 3 and grades 3-5 on November 10. October 23: Elementary school reopening is delayed from November 3 until December 1. Eleven days before the planned school reopening, Supt. Booker announces the district is unable to create a master schedule. November 9: Alameda County allows secondary schools to reopen with protocols in place. November 12: Ms. Cowan’s SPED Learning Center welcomes back five students to Wildwood Elementary School. November 13: Millennium High School welcomes small cohorts of students on campus. November 16: Piedmont’s reopening plan for elementary schools on December 1 is canceled. Alameda County enters the purple tier due to a spike in COVID-19 cases. Schools that have not started by November 17 are not allowed to open. Schools that are already in session may continue. November 17: Nine Transitional Kindergarten (TK) students have their first day of School. December 1: A survey sent to parents to choose in-person or distance learning sparks many complaints. The distance learning option includes an undiscussed or consented to movement to an online “Edgenuity” program. Parent disapproval leads Booker to cancel the plan and the survey. December 30: Newsom introduces “Safe Schools For All” plan with financial incentives for elementary schools that open in February or March. Restrictions are lessened on reopening. To reopen a school’s county need only be under 25 new COVID cases per day instead of seven. January 27, 2021: Teachers and PUSD reach a tentative agreement on reopening. January 31: Booker submits the required COVID Safety Plan to the state and county. February 2: COVID case rates drop to 23.1 new cases per day, opening the door for Alameda County elementary schools to reopen. February 8: Teachers become eligible for COVID-19 vaccine. February 9-11: Grades K-2 return to school for two hours and fifteen minutes per day, four days a week (Tuesday through Friday). February 23: 6th graders return to class for two and a half hours of class per week. February 24: A group of Piedmont parents in an online Reopening Advocacy group conduct a survey of 406 families about their likeliness to stay in the school district. The group asks for a guarantee from PUSD that schools will be fully open in the fall. February 23-25: Grades 3-5 return to school for two hours and fifteen minutes per day Tu-F. March 9: Alameda County enters the red tier of Covid restrictions. Secondary schools can reopen March 10. March 9: The Reopening Advocates distribute over 400 lawn signs reading “OPEN OUR SCHOOLS.” March 16: Exactly one year after closing, grades 9-10 return for eight hours 45 minutes of class every other week (average of four hours 22.5 minutes per week). March 16-19: Grades 7-8 return for two periods of class per week (two and a half hours). March 23: 11th and 12th graders return to school (average of four hours, 22.5 minutes per week). March 25: PUSD commits to opening school full time in fall. A joint statement is signed by Booker, School Board members and representatives of the Piedmont unions

articles.text: Chabot Space & Science Center in new partnership with NASA A new partnership between Chabot Space & Science Center in Oakland and NASA’s Ames Research Center in Mountain View now underway. Anchoring the partnership is a new visitor center called “The NASA Experience” and opening at Chabot in November this year. Under the terms of a 5-year Space Act Agreement, the organizations are beginning a longterm collaboration to create accessible STEAM (science, technology, engineering, art, and math) community engagement and education opportunities in Oakland and beyond. “We are delighted to have this opportunity to bring a deeper NASA experience into our surrounding communities,” said Eugene Tu, director of Ames. “It’s one of NASA’s founding functions to share our work as widely as possible, and this partnership for a new visitor’s center will allow us to reach more broadly than we’d ever be able to do with our existing resources and location in the South Bay.” NASA and Chabot have identified three main areas for immediate collaboration that will use the strengths of NASA’s research and Chabot’s long-standing programs. “We are so excited to share the fascinating science, extraordinary people and groundbreaking research of NASA’s Ames Research Center right here in Oakland,” said Adam Tobin, Executive Director at Chabot Space & Science Center, “Bringing together NASA Ames’ long legacy of innovation and Chabot’s 137-year history in STEM education creates a powerful opportunity to inspire the next generation of future scientists, engineers and astronomers.” “The NASA Experience” creates an immersive, dynamic, STEAM lear ning environment that puts the visitor into the role of a NASA researcher. Hands-on STEAM studios highlight the current science at NASA through interactive challenges, models, artifacts, and more. The visitor center brings to life the challenging and inspiring process of scientific discovery by showcasing the real stories and people at NASA’s Ames Research Center. The two groups will create an interconnected network of STEAM education experiences throughout the city that deepens Chabot’s existing “Learning Everywhere” initiative. Building on existing connections with Oakland’s schools, libraries, and local organizations, this partnership will create programs that engage learners in current NASA research. The partnership will create tangible STEAM career pathways by developing connections between NASA’s career opportunities and Chabot’s youth development programs. NASA will provide speakers, field trips, and independent study on the missions and technology associated with work happening at NASA Ames in collaboration with Chabot’s Galaxy Explorers program, first established in 2000. Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth. NASA’s Ames Research Center, one of 10 NASA field centers across the country, is located in the heart of California’s Silicon Valley. Since 1939, Ames has led NASA in conducting world-class research and development in aeronautics, exploration technology, and science aligned with the center’s core capabilities.

Hands-on STEAM studios highlight the current science at NASA through interactive challenges, models, artifacts, and more. The visitor center brings to life the challenging and inspiring process of scientific discovery by showcasing the real stories and people at NASA’s Ames Research Center. The two groups will create an interconnected network of STEAM education experiences throughout the city that deepens Chabot’s existing “Learning Everywhere” initiative. Building on existing connections with Oakland’s schools, libraries, and local organizations, this partnership will create programs that engage learners in current NASA research. The partnership will create tangible STEAM career pathways by developing connections between NASA’s career opportunities and Chabot’s youth development programs. NASA will provide speakers, field trips, and independent study on the missions and technology associated with work happening at NASA Ames in collaboration with Chabot’s Galaxy Explorers program, first established in 2000. Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth. NASA’s Ames Research Center, one of 10 NASA field centers across the country, is located in the heart of California’s Silicon Valley. Since 1939, Ames has led NASA in conducting world-class research and development in aeronautics, exploration technology, and science aligned with the center’s core capabilities. articles.text: “If you look good, you feel good. If you feel good, you play good. If you play good, they pay good,” stated Football Hall of Fame player Deion Sanders While academic and athletic achievement certainly differ, the premise behind this saying can be applied to test taking, speeches and schoolwork in general. In some respects, taking a test is no different than a sporting match. A game or match is the big stage. It’s the time to play “good” to get paid “good.” In school the games are tests, and the payments are A’s, a G.P.A, and scores of 100. In 2003, Dan Bonin, then a Geometry teacher at Piedmont High, preached the same philosophy on test day. He even offered bonus points to students who dressed up for midterms and finals. Why? It’s all about confidence. –Football Hall of Fame player Deion Sanders It is well known that test scores do not necessarily reflect a student’s comprehension or mastery of course material. This is why the SAT and class grades are not the only factors on college applications. Extra circular activities and essay writing on topics outside of class material can be just as important as numeric scores. Even with comparable understanding of class materials, some students seem to be “good test takers,” or the opposite, kids who “just don’t test well.” Becoming a good test taker is not something you are born with – it is a learned skill. It can be as simple as confidence, demeanor and patience. Looking sharp in an ironed shirt, and tie or in a sophisticated ensemble can be just the edge a B student needs to ace the exam. It’s not about hiding a flash card on the underside of a tie; it is a small investment in self-respect There is something to be said about the effectiveness of school uniforms. Choosing to look snazzy on test day can help your score. and looking the part that can be a major boon on test day. “Look your best” is not an old wives’ tale. It is rooted in psychology and is a tried and true method. I encourage every student to just give it a try on their next big test. Merely taking yourself and the task at hand seriously sets the stage for success. When you look good, you feel good. When you feel good, you are more confident. A tough question early on in an exam has less of a chance to derail your train of thought. Some of the enemies when taking a test include: 1) test material 2) distractions 3) your own mind Some tests require patience to prevent you from breaking concentration which can cause students to miss questions they actually know, or fail to make educated guesses. Another sports mantra, “practice like you play,” can be applied when studing, doing homework, and taking practice tests. In golf, that means going through your normal routine on the driving range before every shot and always picking a target. If a test is going to be timed, time yourself at home. If a test is without the use of a calculator, then attempt to solve problems the same way. A simple thing like wearing polished dress shoes or lucky socks has nothing to do with your feet scoring points on the test. The practice may seem like a superstition but goes beyond that into the realm of the psyche. A picture is worth a thousand words, so look picture- perfect and see what you get in return. Hugh Craig married Inez Gilcrest in 1875, and they raised six children in Piedmont: Evelyn, Roy, Margery, Jessie, Colin, and Eric. In 1954, Evelyn Craig Pattiani published her memoir, Queen of the Hills, about growing up in Piedmont. Craig hired Samuel Bugbee in 1879 to build a house on his acreage on Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue) for $5,000. Architect Bugbee designed the house as a Stick Italianate. It is completely built of redwood with square window bays, vertical siding, and tall narrow windows. Until 1912, the house faced Vernal Avenue and was surrounded by lawns, flower beds, and fruit trees – peach, apricot, plum, and cherry. The water tower had a windmill that pumped the water 50-feet up to the tank to provide water pressure for the house. There was a stable for horses, a barn for cows, and pens for chickens, turkeys, and pigs. It was essentially a self-sustaining farm, as were all the houses in Piedmont in the 1880s. Craig commuted to his insurance office in San Francisco by horsecar and ferry. He said that on a good day, it took 1½ hours to get to the office. The ferry rides On September 5, 1907, Piedmonters again voted on whether to remain a city or to dis-incorporate and become part of Oakland. This time, as a municipality, the vote to dis-incorporate required a two-thirds vote. Of the 154 voters, 92 voted to dis-incorporate, and 62 voted against. Despite the majority vote, those voting to dis-incorporate failed to carry the required two-thirds majority. Piedmont continued as a municipality. A vote of 102 to dis-incorporate would have carried the measure. Just 10 votes made the difference between Piedmont remaining a city or becoming part of Oakland. In those early years, the new city of Piedmont had many issues to solve. The city needed a City Hall, street maintenance, sewer systems, water service, and police and fire protection. How to fund these services? Prior to incorporating, residents paid just one small tax to the County. Owners of city-sized lots paid the same tax as those who owned large acreage. To fund city services, Craig instituted a tax based on the size of the property. The large landowners were not happy with their increased taxes and complained bitterly to Mayor Craig. The taxes remained, but Craig was not re-elected in 1914. Mayor Craig was also a victim of the increased tax basis. He owned six acres and his house was in the middle of his land. In 1912, he moved his house and sub-divided his land. The house was put on log rollers and slowly moved by horses to the corner of Craig’s property where it is now, at 55 Craig Avenue at the corner of Mountain Avenue. Craig then created Craig Avenue with residential lots on both sides of the street. Who was Hugh Craig? Hugh Craig was born in Sydney, Australia in 1841 to Scottish parents. articles.text: You can thank Hugh Craig if you like living in Piedmont and not in Oakland. The San Francisco earthquake and fire in 1906 left most San Franciscans homeless. They fled to Oakland and the East Bay by ferry, and many decided to stay and build their homes here. To accommodate the earthquake refugees, Oakland began annexing as much land as possible. Oakland Mayor Mott spoke to Piedmont residents extolling the advantages of becoming part of “Greater Oakland.” He promised better sewers and roads, improved water supply, and police and fire protection. Oakland politicians thought that annexing the beauty of the Piedmont hills would be a great asset for Oakland. Taxes on the Piedmont land would swell the Oakland coffers. But a group of far-sighted Piedmont residents realized that if they did not do something, they would become part of Oakland. In a race between annexation and incorporation, Piedmont had to move quickly. To incorporate, the city had to have boundaries. With no time for a survey, Hugh Craig and others accepted the northern edge of Oakland as the southern boundary of Piedmont, and the eastern edge of Oakland as the western boundary of Piedmont. With this Seal of Incorporation, Piedmont became an official municipality on January 31, 1907. Hugh Craig was Mayor of Piedmont from 1907 to 1914. The north and east boundaries of the already existing Piedmont Sanitary District completed Piedmont’s boundaries. (This hastily drawn map explains why some Piedmont houses straddle the city lines.) On January 7, 1907, Hugh Craig and James Ballentine raced to Sacramento to file the map of Piedmont, and on Saturday, January 26, 1907, Piedmonters voted to incorporate as a municipality. The Oakland Tribune reported that 117 votes were cast: 79 Piedmont men voted for incorporation, and 38 men voted against. (Women would not be able to vote until 1920.) James Ballentine was elected as Piedmont’s first City Clerk, and five trustees were elected: George Armstrong, Henry Butters, Hugh Craig, Varney Gaskill, and Miles Standish. The trustees surprisingly elected Varney Gaskill as President of the Board of Trustees over Hugh Craig who had led the movement to incorporate. On January 31, 1907, the State of California stamped the documents making Piedmont an official municipal corporation.

They felt the question of cityhood should go before the voters again. With this Seal of Incorporation, Piedmont became an official municipality on January 31, 1907. Hugh Craig was Mayor of Piedmont from 1907 to 1914. The north and east boundaries of the already existing Piedmont Sanitary District completed Piedmont’s boundaries. (This hastily drawn map explains why some Piedmont houses straddle the city lines.) On January 7, 1907, Hugh Craig and James Ballentine raced to Sacramento to file the map of Piedmont, and on Saturday, January 26, 1907, Piedmonters voted to incorporate as a municipality. The Oakland Tribune reported that 117 votes were cast: 79 Piedmont men voted for incorporation, and 38 men voted against. (Women would not be able to vote until 1920.) James Ballentine was elected as Piedmont’s first City Clerk, and five trustees were elected: George Armstrong, Henry Butters, Hugh Craig, Varney Gaskill, and Miles Standish. The trustees surprisingly elected Varney Gaskill as President of the Board of Trustees over Hugh Craig who had led the movement to incorporate. Hugh Craig married Inez Gilcrest in 1875, and they raised six children in Piedmont: Evelyn, Roy, Margery, Jessie, Colin, and Eric. In 1954, Evelyn Craig Pattiani published her memoir, Queen of the Hills, about growing up in Piedmont. Craig hired Samuel Bugbee in 1879 to build a house on his acreage on Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue) for $5,000. Architect Bugbee designed the house as a Stick Italianate. It is completely built of redwood with square window bays, vertical siding, and tall narrow windows. Until 1912, the house faced Vernal Avenue and was surrounded by lawns, flower beds, and fruit trees – peach, apricot, plum, and cherry. The water tower had a windmill that pumped the water 50-feet up to the tank to provide water pressure for the house. There was a stable for horses, a barn for cows, and pens for chickens, turkeys, and pigs. It was essentially a self-sustaining farm, as were all the houses in Piedmont in the 1880s. In 1912, he moved his house and sub-divided his land. articles.text: Cain’s 2 touchdowns give him 14 total TDs in 5-game season The Piedmont High football team finished its shortened fivegame season undefeated, 5-0, after defeating Kennedy High 14-12 at Witter Field on Friday, April 16. It was an emotional victory for the Highlanders after having to drastically reduce its offseason program and losing significant players to the overlapping baseball season. There was no football season in the fall of 2020, due to the COVID-19 health restrictions. In the school’s last full football season, the team posted a 3-7 record in 2019. The game against Kennedy was close. “We had to get all the butterflies out and settle down. We got caught with some penalties but ran the ball well and executed well defensively. I don’t care if we win by two, or one point; we just need to win,” said coach Jerome Johnson. Success is not a foreign concept to this group of players; a majority of whom played on the Undefeated JV team in 2018. “It was a whole team-effort,” explained Ben Marshburn, who plays receiver, safety, and kicker. “Brian [Cain] and our lines have been doing great all year. It’s amazing to have this group of seniors. We have so much chemistry on the field.” “All I was thinking about earlier on Friday was the first day of football when coach [Dick] Carter took a picture of this group [on the JV team]. I looked at that photo earlier and I knew that I was as happy today as I was in that picture,” said quarterback Tommy McNeal. Cain, the talented running back, scored both Piedmont touchdowns with 119 rushing yards on 30 carries. He finishes the 5-game season with 721 rushing yards and 14 touchdowns, averaging nearly 6 yards a carry and 144 yards per game. He was on pace to rush for 1,442 yards in a typical 10-game season. “I can’t give enough credit to the guys up front,” Cain said, thanking the offensive linemen. “They created my running lanes each year. Just to play for them and come through every week is the best feeling.” But for yet another game, it was Johnson’s defense getting the job done. Piedmont defenders had 10 tackles for losses from eight different players, plus three quarterback sacks. The defense twice stopped Kennedy scoring drives near the end zone. Quarterback Tommy McNeil has helped lead Piedmont to an undefeated season. Piedmont’s defense got the job done one more time, holding Kennedy to 12 points in a key victory for the Highlanders. articles.text: Highlanders beat rivals O’Dowd 12-11 in classic match It was a classic barnburner between Piedmont and Bishop O’Dowd’s girls’ lacrosse team on Monday, April 19 at the Dragons’ home field, with the Highlanders coming away victorious in a heated one-goal decision, 12-11. It marked the closest time the Dragons came to unseating the Highlanders in Foothill Division rivalry since BOD won the WACC Championship 10-9 on May 5, 2017. “It’s a fun rivalry. We’re coming off of Spring Break and many girls didn’t pick up a stick for over a week. It was really reaching down and being really gutsy,” said Piedmont coach Carlton Chan. Since Chan took over as head coach in 2019, Piedmont has dominated the series of games with their primary rival. Piedmont has a six-game winning streak against the Dragons dating back to the 2017 WACC title game with former coach Emily Hook. “It was [O’Dowd’s] senior night. They had some loud fans here and their boys’ team heckling us from the side. It’s really a mental game against O’Dowd,” added senior captain Sadie Tschider. articles.text: The Piedmont Center for the Arts opened its 7th Annual Juried Art show last weekend on April 17. Three winners and three honorable mention works of art have been announced. A total of 35 pieces of art were selected among a record-high 500 submissions. The artwork that appeared in the exhibition, the first public event PCA has held this year, was selected by Piedmont native Rene de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Artists came from nine counties in the Bay Area, from Alameda to Santa Clara to Sonoma. Submissions represented an eclectic range, including oil on canvas, pigment prints, and photography. The Juried Art show debuted in November 2013, explained Valerie Corvin, the Juried Art Show curator since its founding. The annual event is made possible through an endowment created by the family of the late John P. Thornborrow. Cash prizes totaling $4,000 are awarded to the top three artists. John Thornborrow was a Bay Area artist who created hundreds of artworks across a variety of mediums. In 2008, his work was selected for the Pro Arts Juried Annual, which was juried by Laura Hoptman, Senior Curator of the New Museum in New York. He continued to produce artwork until his death in 2011. His print, “Fake Flowers,” is on permanent display at the annual show in Piedmont. John Thornborrow Every year, the Juried Art show aims to give emerging artists from the Bay Area an opportunity to gain exposure with top curators and gallerists and the general public,” Corvin said. 2021 Award Winners • First place winner Pep Ventosa was awarded $2,500 for “Watching the Night Sky” • Second place: $1,000 to Tamara Avery for “#114 Justice?” • Third place: See C Oh, $500 for “Tranquility” Honorable Mention Four honorable mentions were also awarded: • Brian Molyneaux’s photograph displayed on metal, “Moon, Neferttiti, Barry” • Nelson Loskamp’s “Cay on the Beach” • Daniel San Souci’s “Flight of the Monarchs.” • Hadi Aghaee’s “Chaos Before The Storm” Honorable mention winners receive ribbons. Corvin said that the selections this year have produced the “best Juried Art Show yet” in the event’s seven-year existence. “The art is a high level, and it feels like you are in a downtown art gallery. It’s very exciting,” added Corvin. The exhibition will be on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, at 801 Magnolia Avenue, on Saturdays and Sundays through May 16. Gallery hours are 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. each day. Visitors need to sign up before their visit, and the exhibition will be limited to a maximum of 20 visitors at a time. Visitors will be asked to sanitize hands upon entry, wear face masks, and observe social distancing. To view the exhibit, register at: https://bit.ly/3mwWuwT. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Crip Camp: A Disability Revolution, is a film nominated for an Oscar for Best Documentary feature and is co-directed by Nicole Newnham, a nearby Oakland resident. The film opens with a long introduction to a unique summer camp called Jened, located in the Catskills a few hours north of New York City. From the 1950s through the 1970s, Crip Camp was a place for teens with a spectrum of disabilities (from polio to cerebral palsy), its purpose was to create an embracing community in which the campers no longer existed on the fringes of society as an invisible minority, but were welcomed, and viewed as far more than one dimensional individuals. The mantra was that everyone mattered, the intent being to offer the quintessential camp experience of dances, baseball games, flirtations, messy bunks, and accessibility to all. You can almost hear their voices calling out, “Yahoooo!” Using archival footage from Camp Jened, shot in the 70s by the People’s Video Theater, this compelling film reminds us that prior to the late 1970s, Americans with disabilities were excluded from schools, public places that were ill-equipped to receive them, and many were denied jobs for which they were qualified. Crip Camp is actually two narratives: The first focuses on a cohort of disabled teens who, in the early 1970s, came to Jened and formed a summer community, days rife with joy and mutual respect, crafting connections that would endure well beyond camp. For many, the Jened experience was revelatory, life changIn 1971 Camp Jened sparked the disability rights movement in America. Documentary filmmakers Nicole Newnham and Jim LeBrecht. ing, a place where they were seen not as one-dimensional individuals who had to confront the assumptions and prejudices of the greater society, but where their disabilities were treated with a shrug, telling them that their handicaps were challenging but not disqualifying. Camp Crip is an extraordinary look at the power of a life experience that throws into relief the contrasting differences between how life was for the disabled and how it could be. And it is that “could be” which represents a dramatic shift in the point of view of Crip Camp, for the campers and the audience. The second part of the film shows the alumni of Jened taking the essence and spirit of Jened to Berkeley, where they form a radical disability movement, a second community of activists and organizers who insisted that legislators see them – really see them – for the first time. Setting up a base in Berkeley’s Center for Independent Living, they worked to find services, jobs, and housing for the disabled, led by Crip Camp alumna Judy Heumann. They also made the strategic decision in 1977 to occupy for 28 days the federal building that housed the Health, Education and Welfare offices. It was a classic protest, and, to their surprise, the occupiers received the support of churches, unions, and advocacy groups including the Black Panthers, some offering supplies and meals. Soon politicians, local and national, began to listen, and, remarkably, change began to take hold. Life for the disabled was reimagined, and equality demanded. This was in reality a civil rights journey for the Jened revolutionaries. Change comes about slowly, but the final result did arrive two decades later with the Americans With Disabilities Act (1999), which proved to be transformative. A f inal comment: Jim Albrecht, who wrote and directed Crip Camp: A Disability Revolution, along with Nicole Newnham, was born with spina bifida. He attended Camp Jened as a teenager where he found he was treated like an ordinary teen, absent even a hint of reflexive discomfort or condescension. “What we saw at that camp,” he said, “was that our lives could be better. You don’t have anything to strive for, if you don’t know it exists.” The 93rd Academy Awards ceremony will be held on April 25 and will include films released between January 1, 2020 and February 28, 2021. There will be no in-person attendance. Crip Camp: A Disability Revolution (2020). Documentary. Written and directed by Jim LeBrecht, Nicole Newnham. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Alicia Vikander as Ava in Ex Machina. Review by Chris Honoré Be prepared to be captivated (or puzzled or creepily moved) by a stylish film that not only constructs a compelling glimpse into the future but asks some big questions along the way. What does it mean to be fully human? Can edgy, idiosyncratic computer geeks/engineers ever create A.I. machines (call them animatronics) that possess a brain that doesn’t just store information, no matter how sophisticated, but can respond to questions posed with a startling self-awareness? Ex Machina opens with Caleb (Domhall Gleeson), an employee of a Google-like company, flying in a helicopter to the remote, mountainous retreat of the company’s owner, Nathan (Oscar Isaac). He will spend a week involved in what is called a “Turing test.” Upon his arrival – the home is constructed of steel and concrete and glass, beautiful yet stark, built into a mountain – he is briefed by Nathan about his mission. Caleb will be conducting a series of interviews with a robot named Ava (Alicia Vikander). She has a human form, her body transparent, revealing her inner circuitry, and possesses a gorgeous face and a soft, seductive voice. Caleb is tasked with determining whether Ava can cross that boundary that differentiates man from machine. Is she conscious of the difference between Caleb and herself? He sits in a glass walled room, Ava on one side of a window of sorts and Caleb on the other. Nathan is watching and recording the interactions. It is a fascinating series of conversations and it soon becomes clear that Caleb is drawn to Ava. Her humanity, so to speak, attracts him. Her preternatural responses are enigmatic, varied, demonstrating a curiosity about him that he finds appealing and surprising. The above doesn’t begin to describe how strangely creative this film is, how remarkably different. The characters, to include Ava, are remote, bright, inaccessible, yet maddeningly flawed and revealing. Nathan delivers a fraternal, let’s be bros patter with an embedded menace that makes Caleb feel relaxed, at least initially, and then increasingly uneasy as each day passes. The setting is simultaneously austere and yet welcoming, the trees seeming to be part of the house’s modern and sparse interior. There is a sense of bonhomie and beauty layered with a chilling detachment (Ex Machina was filmed in a mountainous region of Norway). There is also a question woven into the narrative: how do we define our own humanity? What makes us unique, as distinguished from other life forms on the planet? We know there are those among us who seem to have flatlined, as if they had been in retreat all of their lives. And yet there are those who, in the alternative, burn with a life force and possess a certain spark. Many glow with a humanity that can astonish when they engage. They possess qualities that can seem indefinable. Whatever it is, we know it when we encounter it. And it is that experience with Ava that gives Caleb pause while he marvels at what Nathan has achieved. Clearly her intelligence exceeds his. And yet, he also feels surrounded by a sense of corruption, that much of what he is told is a distortion and that he is being manipulated. The question is, by whom? Ex Machina. Directed by Alex Garland. Starring Domhall Gleeson, Oscar Isaac and Alicia Vikander. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated R. Domhall Gleeson and Oscar Isaac in a scene from Ex Machina.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Frozen II, released in 2019, was the sequel to Disney’s hugely popular Frozen from six years earlier. It was an Oscar-winning animated film featuring not only a compelling story of sister empowerment, but songs that still stand alone. Sequels are often a gamble for any studio and the bar had been set high with the first Frozen. But the sequel proved to be family-friendly, and again sought out and found the target audience (young girls, especially), while incorporating not only strong role model relationships, but a touch of romance, comedy and adventure, all blended with new songs that fit the narrative. The challenge for the creators of Two was to tell a new story that, while relying on the first Frozen, would be fresh and engaging, with elements found in the extraordinary work of Japanese animator Hayao Miyazaki of Studio Ghibli. The story opens in that familiar terrain of the original Frozen. Queen Elsa (Idina Menzei), has regained her magical powers, and now rules over the peaceful kingdom of Arendelle. Her sister, Princess Anna (Kristen Bell), offers advice and encouragement. The two have an unbreakable bond. And there is ice-cutter Kristoff (Jonathan Groffer) who is planning to ask for Anna’s hand in marriage, though he can’t seem to get the proposal right. Meanwhile, Snowman Olaf (Josh Gad), immune to melting, offers continual comic relief. Though Arendelle is tranquil, dark forces are gathering, emanating from an enchanted and mysterious forest. Queen Elsa must penetrate the shroud of misty fog that surrounds the woods, subdue the power therein, and reveal the secret that threatens the kingdom. Frozen II is reliant on superb CGI animation and imagery, with crisp colors that are stunningly realistic, bringing the vistas and the characters into dramatic relief. Musically, the new material mirrors the original, and the songs, which fit nicely into the narrative. Frozen II. Disney Animation. Directed by Chris Buck & Jennifer Lee. With the voices of Kristen Bell, Idina Menzei, Josh Gad and Jonathan Groff. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré If you have some youngsters hanging around the house and you haven’t taken them to see A Wrinkle in Time, pile them in the car and insist they see it on the big screen. It’s a gorgeous film, a solid adventure, and while the kids will easily access their sense of wonder, well, reach for yours as well. As an adult I acknowledge that the most interesting part of the story for me was act one when Meg Murray (Storm Reid) is introduced. She’s a 13-year-old middle schooler who has developed an attitude that gets her either picked on by her school’s Mean Girls or results in a visit to the principle’s office. In truth Meg has been grieving for the last four years due to the baffling disappearance of her beloved father, Dr. Alex Murray (Chris Pine), a physicist. Meg is clearly gifted, though she suffers from a damaged self-image and sense of self-worth. Her mother (Gugu MbathaRaw), also a physicist, is equally devastated by the loss of her husband, and is upset with Meg. It’s only Meg’s brother, Charles Wallace (Deric McCabe), who has made some friends who he is convinced can assist them in finding their father. As it turns out, Calvin, from Storm Reid stars in A Wrinkle in Time. Meg’s school, shows up one day and is around when Charles’ new acquaintances reveal themselves: think of them as the three Missus – Mrs. Which (Oprah Winfrey), Mrs. Whatsit (Reese Witherspoon) and Mrs. Who (Mindy Kaling). They are celestial, ephemeral beings that agree to help Meg and Charles Wallace and Calvin find Dr. Murray. And so off they go, into the farthest parts of the universe. It’s quite a journey and one that first introduces kids to a planet of light. It’s there they confront the IT, which represents the dark side of life – a threatening essence that the three must face alone and likely has Meg’s father. Mrs. Which tells them that IT is spreading through the universe and to be careful. Remember – this is a kids’ movie and therefore has as its premise a complete suspension of disbelief. An example is the word “tessering,” meaning a wrinkle in time and the way that the three Mrs. and Meg, et al. travel across the universe. It proves to be a great trip (and back) filled with lessons for all of them. Kids of all ages will enjoy A Wrinkle in Time, but especially tweens and younger. A Wrinkle in Time. Starring Storm Reid, Chris Pine and Oprah Winfrey. Directed by Ava DuVernay. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. Reese Witherspoon, Oprah Winfrey, and Mindy Kaling as the three Muses in A Wrinkle in Time.

articles.text: University of California Botanical Garden in Berkeley. University of California, Berkeley’s Botanical Garden has an impressive display of Southern African flora and fauna now in bloom. Thousands of vividly colored flowers – in hues of yellow, purple, orange, fuchsia and white – cover the hillsides of the botanical garden. This spring is an excellent time to see the floral display in the designated Southern African area of the gardens. Annuals, succulents, and geophytes, or plants that grow from bulbs, are now blooming in abundance in the botanical garden’s Karoo beds. South African plants include natives of South Africa, Lesotho, Swaziland, Botswana and Namibia. The plants of this region of the African continent are famous for their diversity of fauna, owing to the diverse typography and climate. The blooms have also attracted a variety of pollinators. Garden staff have noted two bird species, Hooded Orioles and Bushtits, have gravitated to the floral beds, and can be seen sipping nectar from their preferred candelabra aloe. Visitors have just two weeks to see these blooms in full force. Many of the featured spring bulbs and annuals bloom mostly in February and May. Advance ticketing is required. Modified hours are observed, although the garden is open daily. Members-only hour is 10 a.m. to 11 a.m., and general admission is available from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Note that there will be path disruptions throughout the garden, as staff manages visitation flow as per Center for Disease Control guidelines. Glasshouses and water fountains are temporarily closed. To obtain tickets, visit: https:// botanicalgarden.berkeley.edu/ covid-reopen.

articles.text: On view: Do Ho Suh’s “Karma” and Pae White’s “Noisy Blushes” The San Jose Museum of Art (SJMA) is open to the public three days a week, Friday through Sunday. Two new exhibitions will be on view: Do Ho Suh’s “Karma” and Pae White’s “Noisy Blushes.” April 22 is the last day to see “Barring Freedom”, an exhibit co-organized by UC Santa Cruz Institute of the Arts and Sciences and the museum. The exhibition confronts the historical and structural racism that is embedded in the United States’ criminal justice and mass incarceration systems. It has been on display since the museum’s reopening last month. White’s “Noisy Blushes” (2020) serves as a meditation on movement and time, light and color; as well as actual material presence and form. The artwork was commissioned by the San Jose Museum of Art and fills the building’s 30-foot-tall atrium to transform the entrance for visitors. Do Ho Suh’s “Karma,” a 23-foot tower of bronze male figures stacked on top of one another perched on top of each other’s shoulders, will be on display through January 30, 2022. The museum has exhibits for youth as well. articles.text: Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will present its annual spring recital on May 8. The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choirs’ youngest choral groups, the Kinder and Training departments, will present their 2021 spring recital on Saturday, May 8. This recital will showcase the departments’ progress in their choral training, and also will feature virtual choir performances from the six ensembles within both departments. The concert will live-stream via YouTube at 4 p.m. The kinder choir consists of students ages five and six. Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir introduces intermediate music skills to students grades one and up in the training department, the second echelon of the three-department program. After graduating from the kinder department, students move on to the training department, where they deepen their understanding of dictation, music theory, and beginning stage presence. They also expand their musical literacy and begin to learn how to sight read. Many other basic skills are solidified here, such as ear training, breath control, and vowel formation. These skills are necessary as young students’ voices begin to mature. The kinder and training departments will join the older performing department on June 5 for the annual “Spring Sing!” Over 200 singers from all ten of the organizations’ departments will present this special choral performance. Both events are free to watch; because of the generosity of patrons, Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir is able to offer its entire 2020-21 “Discovering our Voices” virtual concert season free to the public via YouTube. Donations are gratefully received to help offset production costs. For more information, and to register on Eventbrite for the event, visit https://www.piedmontchoirs. org/event-calendar.
articles.title: All PEBCC vocalists in finale concert on June 5

articles.text: Gold Coast Chamber Players’ season finale, “Dvorak’s America” on Saturday, May 1, will conclude their collection of virtual concerts. “Dvorak’s America” explores the impact that Spirituals and Native American music had on Czech composer Antonin Dvorak during his time in America. The project, three years in the making, highlights the interconnectedness of these cultures. The program will feature the composer’s Sting Quintet, op. 97, and the Lento from his String Quartet op. 96, both of which are nicknamed “the American.” Original music by Mary Youngblood for Native American flute, “Within My Heart” and “Beneath the Raven Moon,” as well as her arrangement of “Amazing Grace”, represent what Dvorak heard during his stay in America. Dvorak proclaimed that African American Spirituals are “the heart of American music,” and the genre serves as perhaps the greatest Western influence on the composer. Spirituals that will be performed in this program include “Swing Low Sweet Chariot,” “By an’ By,” and “My Lord What a Morning.” ConcludAlexander String Quartet: Zakarias Grafilo and Frederick Lifsitz, violins, Sandy Wilson, cello and violist David Samuel, a recent addition. ing the program will be “Goin’ Home,” from the composer’s New World Symphony. Alexander String Quartet will lead the ensemble, marking one of the first performances with their new violist, David Samuel. Violist Pamela Freund-Striplen, founder of Gold Coast Players and a frequent collaborated with the Quartet, will join its members for “Dvorak’s America.” The event will be livestreamed via YouTube at 7 p.m. on Saturday, May 1. For more information and to obtain tickets, visit www.gccpmusic.com, or call (925) 283-3728.

articles.text: The experience of visiting the Oakland Zoo just got more fun for kids with the announcement that the zoo’s five California Wilds playground areas are opening April 19. The zoo gained approval to reopen the area from Alameda County as a result of the county remaining in the COVID orange tier. The kid-friendly environments are modeled after five unique California habitats. They opened in 2018 when the California Trail area of the zoo doubled the zoo’s acreage. The interactive, and custom playgrounds provide unique play environments within sight of young black, brown and Grizzly bears. The California Wilds playgrounds have their own version of Mt. Shasta with climbing ropes, lava tube tunnels, and a glacier slide. An old growth redwood ring and a babbling stream share the forest zone with a giant bird nest to play in. A desert landscape and bay/ocean zones also serve to teach kids about the local land while having a great time on the rubber safety surfacing. Be on the lookout for the zoo to reopen more areas in the coming weeks. For tickets to visit the zoo and for more information, visit www.oaklandzoo.org.
articles.title: Oakland Zoo reopens five playgrounds for kids

articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters is hosting a public discussion with Alameda County District Attorney Nancy O’Malley on May 6 starting at 4 p.m. She will describe the work by her department with abused and homeless women, helping them move beyond trauma into a positive future. O’Malley will address the many challenges COVID-19 has posed. She will explain the ways in which the current lack of civility in politics is impeding the pace and scale of progress for women who suffer from violence. For example, passage of the Violence Against Women Act was held up due to politics, and funding for the Victims Crime Act, which provides resources to states for victims of crime, was also reduced. O’Malley is a nationally recognized expert on issues involving violence against women, violence against persons with disabilities, and interpersonal violence including sexual assault, domestic violence, elder abuse, child abuse, stalking, and human exploitation and trafficking. She serves in the office that dates to a time when Earl Warren was the Alameda County D.A. before becoming United States Supreme Court Chief Justice. O’Malley is the first woman to serve as the County’s District Attorney. articles.text: • • It’s become a mantra. If you want to have a close relationship with your grandchildren and their parents, just zip your lip and open your wallet. I challenge you to find one book, article, or expert who does not advocate this as a first line approach to becoming a new grandparent. When you think about it, who wouldn’t adore you if you never said a word, just smiled lovingly, and supplied them with unlimited funds? No one! But is this really what constitutes a satisfying grandparent-adult child relationship? Satisfying for whom? When the lip is zipped, not only is all the unsolicited advice and criticism silenced, but so too are the accolades, the support, the encouragement, and the loving praise. New parents are learning their role on the job, and they seek information and reassurance from trusted sources all around them. Websites with information and advice about every developmental stage, countless parent advice blogs, baby tracking apps, sleep training books, and their friends and colleagues with children are all constantly being polled. Reviews of every baby and child product are scoured before a purchase is made. And once polled, decisions about their children are made with confidence. Once these choices and decisions are made, then what? It’s normal to look for affirmation that you’re doing a good job at something that you care about. Perhaps a grandparent unzipping the lip is just what new parents need? Sometimes finding just the right words can be difficult. But with authentic intention, and not mere flattery, specific feedback is almost always welcome. Examples: • When the baby was appearing inconsolable and screaming this morning, I watched you soothe him calmly and confidently. This allowed his big sister to continue playing without interruption or distraction. • You walked in the door yesterday after a rough day of work, and immediately and joyfully engaged with your daughter and began to play with her. She is learning that she is always the most important part of your day. The meals that you plan for your children every day are balanced and healthy. These meals keep the kids really well satisfied and it’s clear that they are not hyped up on sugar or additives. You have a reliable bedtime ritual for the children that is relaxing and predictable for them. I can see that it helps them to prepare for going to bed and I bet it’s why they sleep so well through the night. Do young parents really want silent grandparents? Of course, they don’t. What they want and need is support, reassurance, and positive feedback. They want the freedom to raise their children in the manner that feels right to them. They don’t want to be judged by yesterday’s standards when they live in a world that is almost unrecognizable to the older generation. They need grandparental support, and yes, sometimes the support they need is financial. But more than anything else, they need their parents’ love and acknowledgement that they themselves are doing a great job at being parents. It’s their turn, after all. Piedmont resident Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides, counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@ itstheirturn.com.

articles.text: The other day I saw the U.S. Surgeon General, Vivek H. Murthy interviewed on television. Though he stressed the need to continue following CDC guidelines, he was happy to point out that because of the COVID vaccination successes, “we are seeing the light at the end of the tunnel getting brighter and brighter.” Talk like this gets me excited to think about life getting back to “normal,” though this looks quite different now than it did only a year ago. I know many people are wondering if senior living communities, including assisted living and independent living, are safe to explore again in this “new normal?” Early data appears to show that the highest quality senior living communities adapted quickly and responsibly to COVID-19. They spent the last year implementing prevention measures and determining what healthy socialization looks like for their residents. Some of these plans included new opportunities for indoor exercise and dining, special learning activities, integrating entertainment and providing innovative ways for face-to-face engagement for residents and staff. If you’re not certain that now is the right time to consider a community, ask yourself what has this past year been like for you and those you love? Many older adults have become more isolated because of the necessary precautions that were put in place to prevent the spread of COVID-19. Today, more active older Eleanor, Karma and Gloria enjoy a conversation during a Residents’ Happy Hour at The Lake Merritt Independent Senior Living. adults are making the move to senior living communities as a lifestyle choice. They want to be active in their retirement, relinquish daily tasks and home maintenance, and want to take advantage of the social aspects, custom services, amenities and opportunities created just for them. Researchers have found that older adults who report the highest levels of well-being and happiness are those who socialize, work or volunteer and exercise with others. If you visit an independent living community or an assisted living community, you’ll find residents participating in many different activities, programs and committees. You’ll also find that each community’s culture is shaped by the residents who live there. Diane Broch, the Community Relations Director at The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living community has been getting a lot of calls from people who tell her they have been feeling isolated and are more curious than ever about community living. “We are able to reassure them that our residents interact with each other on a daily basis and are fully vaccinated as are all newcomers to the community,” she explained. “It is a much healthier lifestyle to have a community of fellow residents and staff you can engage with, versus being alone in your home. We follow the CDC guidelines as they are released and really care about each other. Our residents are happy that they can engage with everyone here.” With the light at the end of the tunnel getting brighter, all of us will have an opportunity to reassess our many options for what’s next. As for me, I know I am joined by our residents who are thrilled to be fully vaccinated and who can plan for a more active and involved future. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, at 1800 Madison Street in Oakland. For further information call 510- 903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com.

articles.text: Two extraordinary artists return to Oakland-based arts education company Stagebridge for a session filled with opportunities for elders to take back their stories. With classes starting next week, April 26, Masankho Banda and Sheila Arnold are two incredible instructors sparking creativity in the Performing Arts Institute (PAI) session this Spring “The fact that we have so many returning instructors for Spring 2021 session is a real tribute to our students,” PAI program director Lily Nguyen said. “I’m so happy we can have incredible instructors tapping deeper into everyone’s creativity.” In “Dynamic & Effective Storytelling,” African storyteller Banda teaches an introductory class welcoming everyone interested in turning their memories and experiences into stories for all. The Malawi-born InterPlay Leader tours the world telling stories and teaching the craft of storytelling. He is also a member of the National Association of Black Storytellers (NABS) and the National Storytelling Network (NSN). Concurrently, performer and storytelling instructor Arnold will be teaching “Fairytales, Folklore & Social Justice.” This discussion-based class encourages students to utilize stories to address social issues including poverty, immigration, race reconciliation, PTSD, and more. “…with encouragement and instruction from Sheila Arnold and support of my classmates, I worked at it, saw the light, and wrote my very first fairytale, ‘King LeRoy and Alia,’” student Eleanor Levine said. “I am proud of the way I was able to weave magical twists into my morality tale [about] ending the death penalty.” With this wave of instructors exploring the depths of storytelling, Stagebridge has also offered Storyteller and performer Sheila Arnold leads “Fairytales, Folklore & Social Justice” for Stagebridge’s Spring 2021 Online Performing Arts Institute session. more and more scholarships and one-on-one Zoom coaching for new students, ensuring online classes are accessible to all new students. “Everyone has the ability to be touched by performing arts,” Executive Director Shannon McDonnell said. “And we are always trying to break down all barriers to accessing the magic and joy in our classes.” To register for classes and learn about the full range of activities at Stagebridge, visit www.stagebridge.org. Located at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland (across from Whole Foods), Stagebridge is the nation’s oldest and most renowned theatre company of older adults. For information, call (510) 444-4755.

articles.text: Q: A: Q: Does anyone yearn to be 60? Yes – people who are 70. When should you become worried about incidents of forgetfulness? A: Forgetting your car keys: not a problem. articles.text: Well-meaning family members and friends often give an enthusiastic “Yes!” when someone asks for a little help at home due to age, illness, or other life change that leaves them in need of support. It feels good to help someone and make them happier, after all. However, this temporary commitment can soon expand into something that requires more than they can handle in terms of time, physical strength, or emotional stamina. Injured on the “Job” A family member may offer to help someone simply to step safely out of the tub, and then find themselves with a back injury. There are proper techniques for lifting someone from a chair or bed, or assisting them in the bathroom, which professional caregivers receive training for. A possible solution is to determine which aspects of care seem the riskiest for the person who is helping out, then hire a caregiver to step in for those specific tasks instead. This might mean just an hour or two per day, giving the family member a little break and keeping them safe as well. What’s Burnout? The definition of burnout is “fatigue, frustration, or apathy resulting from prolonged stress, overwork, or intense activity.” When an untrained family member or friend attempts to be a caregiver, while possibly balancing work or family responsibilities, they can burn out. It’s impossible to keep adding more and more to your plate, especially when you don’t really know what to do, or what’s coming next… Eventually the plate comes crashing down. Establishing boundaries is important for family caregivers so that they don’t experience burnout. If they’re not careful other issues can develop while caring for an elder loved one, such as stress at work or with children in the home. Consider asking other friends or family to share the responsibilities of caregiving or hire someone to be part of your care team. Feelings do matter Caregivers can feel resentful, and it’s perfectly natural, especially if they give too much of themselves without much in return. Ideally, a care relationship can involve both give and take so that resentment doesn’t develop. Finding others who are having similar experiences can be helpful for negative feelings affecting a caregiver. There are all kinds of support groups, both online and in person, in which family caregivers can vent, learn, and share. Support groups might be for caregiving in general or for a specific type of caregiving such as for someone who is living with dementia or Parkinson’s disease. These groups may be an offshoot of an organization such as the Alzheimer’s Association or a local church. When a family member or friend begins to experience some of the possible challenges of caregiving, a professional caregiver can step in to ease the burden.
