articles.text: Mayanist scholar, generous researcher of Pre-Columbian art and culture On the beautiful spring afternoon of Sunday, April 18, a quickly organized but lovely gathering formed to grieve, recall, and honor Susan Dutcher of Piedmont. The memorial gathering on her front lawn was put together by her many local friends and adoring neighbors. Also in attendance were Susan’s only two West Coast relatives who came from Reno. The attendance of about 30 included people of all ages. The crowd was addressed casually, informally, and from the heart by about 15 speakers. Everyone wore a mask, even though Piedmonters have the highest vaccination rate in the state. It was heartwarming to hear reminiscences and anecdotes and thereby learn more about Susan and her varied life over about 76 years. Her closest neighbors talked about the many, many nice things she did for them, unasked, appearing like a genie when suitcases, packages, or groceries needed to be carried. Although it was wryly observed that Susan didn’t much waste time cleaning her own house, she would materialize when she could help others. She was also known among neighbors for using her own traffic cones or her battered old truck to save parking spots right in front of neighbors’ houses when they were returning from a trip. When boulevard median strips around town became either overgrown or barren, Susan would appear fearlessly near traffic to garden and plant. She baby-sat local kids for parents who were called away, tutored some kids and read to others, and filled in at games when another playmate was needed to even up teams. She taught math in East Palo Alto for many years as a career. She sponsored her best learners in their continuing education, like personal scholarships. She took it upon herself to provide extra tutoring for those students who needed it. “Quirky” but beloved were adjectives used frequently at the memorial gathering. It was overwhelming to see how strongly she was appreciated by all her neighbors and friends. She knew all the neighbors and their kids, and kept an eye out for them as a block guardian. She knew which college every kid on the block had gone off to and greeted them to inquire about their studies and their college life when they came back home for holidays. Every holiday she received invitations to family meals and celebrations, like everyone’s favorite aunt. Her cause of death is currently unknown. A neighbor reported that she looked peaceful and pain-free when found inside her home. Several Piedmonters wish to honor her by contributing to the several charities she did volunteer work for. She generously helped: Mexican & Guatemalan poor village communities; her school in East Palo Alto; and locally, Bambino, a thrift shop in Oakland run by a nonprofit charity for children., for whom she took care of all the books donated and sold. Susan walked every day to Mulberry’s Market, Piedmont’s only grocery store and central gathering point, for coffee and to chat with others. It was revealed that every Christmas, Susan gave every Mulberry’s employee a $50 bill and sometimes a $100 bill. The owners of Mulberry’s Market are going to put up a plaque honoring Susan’s friendship. Among the 15 speakers at the memorial gathering were about five women who had been friends with Susan since kindergarten, including Piedmont historian Gail Lombardi. A message sent from out of state by old friend Pam Arlett Garzini was read by Nancy DeRoche. Dave DeRoche explained that everyone should realize that Susan Dutcher was one of the world’s top two dozen or so experts on the Maya people, their art, civilization, architecture, written language, and ruins. This ancient culture was one of the world’s greatest and biggest, circa AD 300–900, with a calendar, a writing system, irrigation, and pyramids. Susan explored a large number of Maya ruins in Mexico’s and Guatemala’s steamy jungles, apparently never slowed by the heat and humidity. Susan was an extremely dedicated assistant to, and researcher with, the legendary Mayanist author, photographer, scholar, philanthropist and foundation director Merle Greene Robertson. Susan travelled with Merle on more than 20 trips to Mexico and Guatemala. Greene, said, “My mom was a wonderful person and scholar, but she was so passionate about Mayan research and so energetic (even well into her 80s and 90s) that she could be demanding to work with and hard to travel with. Susan Dutcher got along better with my mother than anyone else on earth. I think this was because of three reasons: they tolerated each other’s quirkiness 100%; they had a mutual admiration society; and Susan would talk to my mother all day long and my mother was deaf as a post.” The Mexican government awarded Merle Greene a Gold Eagle award as a great citizen who did so much for Mexico. It was the equivalent of an honorary Nobel Prize and citizenship. For decades, Merle was considered one of the top ten persons leading Mayan research, conservation, and knowledge. Always alongside was Susan Dutcher as Merle’s volunteer helper, administrative assistant, expedition-planner, conference and lecture-planner, and supportive friend. confirmed that Piedmont currently does not have staff that can coordinate arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. The City of Piedmont’s annual Arbor Day celebration will take place on Friday, April 30, and will be virtual. It will include youth-focused activities, a video that highlights selections of Heritage Trees, and the traditional tree-planting. This year, for the first time, celebrations will include a sidewalk chalk-drawing contest for Piedmont’s younger residents. Children will be encouraged to select their favorite street tree or park tree next to a sidewalk, write the name of the tree in chalk, and then decorate the sidewalk with chalk art to celebrate the tree. Parents can take a photo of the artwork and submit it to Parks Projects Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmint.ca.gov. Prizes will be awarded for the most creative tree art. A 30-minute video is being created with footage of each designated Heritage Tree in Piedmont, including the most recent winners. Heritage Trees will be introduced by the person or the family that nominated them. Zack Parisa will be featured in the video as Arbor Day speaker. Parisa, a Piedmont resident, is the co-founder and CEO of SilviaTerra. SilviaTerra uses Natural Capital Exchange (NCAPX) to provide a marketplace for forest carbon payments. Recently, SilviaTerra collaborated with Microsoft to create “Basemap,” the first high-resolution forest inventory of the United States. The video will be shown live via KCOM on April 30 and will be available to view on the city’s website after then. This year’s traditional Arbor Day tree planting will be the planting of three Yulan Magnolia trees in honor of Ralston Louie, the son of Park Commissioner Robin Wu.
